_comment: Curated selection from the Library of Congress National Jukebox. 'category' and 'note' are curator annotations written for this project (not LoC text); all other metadata is pulled from the LoC JSON API by scripts/01_fetch_loc.py.

items.note: Vess L. Ossman was the most-recorded banjoist of the acoustic era; this is an early Victor recording of a ragtime banjo solo.

Caruso's first Victor session (New York, 1 February 1904) included this aria from Leoncavallo's Pagliacci, accompanied on piano. His Victor recordings helped make the phonograph respectable for classical music.
George M. Cohan's song from the 1904 Broadway musical Little Johnny Jones, recorded in Philadelphia the following year.
Bert Williams, a Black star of vaudeville and later the Ziegfeld Follies, sings a song from Abyssinia (1906), the Williams and Walker musical named in the LoC record.
Geraldine Farrar sang Cio-Cio-San in the Metropolitan Opera's first production of Madama Butterfly (1907), the same year as this recording.
Australian soprano Nellie Melba's aria from Puccini's La Bohème, recorded in New York in 1907 for Victor's premium Red Seal series.
'Take Me Out to the Ball Game' (Norworth/Von Tilzer) was published in 1908; this Columbia recording was made the same summer.
'Red Wing' (Kerry Mills and Thurland Chattaway, 1907) was one of the most popular 'intermezzo' songs of its day; here a male duet with orchestra.
The sextet from Donizetti's Lucia di Lammermoor, sung by a Metropolitan Opera ensemble led by Caruso; Victor sold it as a premium-priced disc.
Irving Berlin's 1911 hit, recorded by the comic duo Arthur Collins and Byron Harlan within months of publication.
'Let Me Call You Sweetheart' (Friedman/Whitson, 1910) in a male-quartet arrangement typical of the period.
Scottish music-hall star Harry Lauder sings one of his signature songs; LoC files it under descriptive specialties and ethnic music.
A Peerless Quartet ragtime song from the height of the pre-war ragtime song craze.

James Reese Europe's Society Orchestra accompanied the dancers Vernon and Irene Castle. Its 1913-14 Victor sessions are among the first recordings by a Black American orchestra; LoC also credits Ford T. Dabney as composer.
W. C. Handy's 'Memphis Blues' (published 1912) sung by Morton Harvey; often cited as one of the earliest vocal recordings of a published blues.
'Poor Butterfly' (Hubbell/Golden) came from the 1916 Hippodrome revue The Big Show.
The Original Dixieland Jazz Band's 'Livery Stable Blues' (Victor, 1917) is widely regarded as the first commercially issued jazz record.
W. C. Handy's own orchestra recorded for Columbia in New York in September 1917, seven months after the ODJB's Victor version of the same tune.
George M. Cohan's First World War anthem 'Over There', sung by vaudeville star Nora Bayes in 1917.
'Tiger Rag', one of the ODJB's best-known numbers, recorded in New York in March 1918.
Enrico Caruso's 1918 recording of 'Over There', sung partly in French, shows an opera star taking on a popular war song.
Ben Selvin's 'Dardanella' was one of the best-selling dance records of the era.
George Gershwin's 'Swanee' became his first major hit after Al Jolson took it up in 1919-20.
'Whispering' (1920) was a major hit. LoC credits the Ambassador Orchestra and lists Paul Whiteman as leader, with Ferde Grofé (piano, arranger) and Henry Busse (trumpet).
The ODJB's 1921 recording of W. C. Handy's 'St. Louis Blues', with a vocal by Al Bernard according to the LoC record.
Arthur Pryor's Band, led by Sousa's former trombone soloist, plays a 'barn dance' arrangement of 'Shine On, Harvest Moon', the Nora Bayes and Jack Norworth hit of 1908.
